analytic.title: Predictable Runtime Monitoring

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Dynamic program monitoring has been applied in software-intensive systems to detect runtime constraint violations and trigger system recovery actions. Uncontrolled monitoring activities may, however, delay detection of a violation for an unbounded time and, worse, affect the original system's schedulability. In this paper, we introduce the concept of predictable monitoring, which demands a bound on detection latency while ensuring temporal noninterference by the monitoring process. We present off-line analysis techniques for predicting the maximum detection latency with fixed-priority scheduling under two types of monitoring schemes: synchronous and asynchronous. For asynchronous monitoring, we illustrate how to achieve predictable monitoring by bounding the detection latency and controlling the monitoring budget using a bandwidthpreserving, server-based approach.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Verifying the correctness of complex embedded systems is a significant challenge, but one that must be pursued to assure the safe operation of the multitude of devices that are to be embedded in future military, transportation, healthcare, and power systems. Despite enormous advances in static verification techniques over the past decades, e.g., model checking [1], the trend towards increasing size and complexity of software in embedded systems promises to make their static verification impractical in the foreseeable future.

To address this limitation, a recent trend in embedded systems is the use of runtime monitoring to verify properties of system executions and to compensate for detected violations. In this approach a monitor executes alongside the program observing its evolving behavior at selected points and judging those observations against a predefined specification. Researchers have investigated the use of this strategy to monitor a diverse set of specifications that impact correct embedded system operation, including, characteristics of hardware failures, e.g., [2], changes in the physical environment, e.g., [3], security attack patterns, e.g., [4], and interface specifications for hardware and software components, e.g., [5].

These efforts can be viewed as the initial steps in adapting results from the mature field of runtime monitoring to consider the challenges of embedded systems verification, but they do not go far enough. A recent analysis of the field surveyed 18 state-of-the-art runtime monitoring techniques and classified them according to 37 different characteristics [6]. Nowhere in this assessment of the field were the specific challenges of runtime monitoring of real-time systems addressed.

We present the concept of predictable runtime monitoring which explicitly addresses two real-time monitoring requirements: (i) that monitor execution does not interfere with the temporal correctness of the underlying system, and (ii) that monitors themselves meet temporal correctness requirements. To illustrate the necessity of these requirements consider the problem of run-time verification of aircraft flight control systems. One strategy [7] deploys a complex controller and a simple, statically verified, controller together on the aircraft. Runtime monitors detect when the aircraft enters states in which the complex controller is not known to be safe and the system reverts to the simpler verified controller. Clearly, the execution of monitors should not interfere with the complex controller to avoid risking loss of control of the aircraft. In addition, the monitor must detect problematic system states quickly enough so that the simpler controller can be activated in time to preserve aircraft safety.

In this paper, we make three technical contributions that define predictable monitoring solutions and explore tradeoffs among those solutions with fixed-priority scheduling. (1) Predictable monitoring requires the explicit definition of a monitoring budget-the share of resources that are dedicated to monitoring; here we consider the temporal monitoring budget, but one could also consider space and power budgets. (2) Systems may use a set of monitors to track different system characteristics and the criticality of a characteristic, and hence of its associated monitors, may vary. To address this we propose the explicit definition of monitor detection latency-a bound on the time between when the system property is violated and when the monitor indicates that violation. (3) In principle, by tolerating a longer detection latency it may be possible to realize systems with smaller monitoring budgets. We propose a bandwidth-preserving, server-based approach to predictable monitoring under fixedpriority scheduling and develop off-line analysis techniques for determining the maximum possible detection latency. We use this approach to explore the relationship between detection latency and monitoring budget.

We focus in this paper on software-based monitoring, since it is the most prevalent approach to runtime monitoring. We note that hardware-based monitoring techniques [8]- [11] can eliminate some of the effects of monitoring activities on the system, but the difficulty of maintenance, portability and scalability, heavily limit the application of hardware-based monitoring [12]. Moreover, another trend is to use hybrid approaches to monitoring that mix software and hardware support [13], [14]; the software components of such solutions must be predictable.

In the next section, we define the key concepts that underly predictable runtime monitoring. Section 3 discusses the parameters that a system designer must consider in determining the budget for monitoring activity. We identify several approaches to achieving bounded detection latency in Section 4 and evaluate tradeoffs between detection latency and monitoring budget in Section 5. We discuss related work and conclude with our plans for the future in Sections 6 and 7.

div.head: Background and Definitions
div.p: Researchers have proposed a variety of property specification formalisms for runtime monitoring [6]. These include formalisms for specifying state properties-which assert conditions on values of program variables at specific locations during program execution-and path properties-which describe proper sequencing of system states or events.

Path-property formalisms for runtime monitoring express safety properties-properties whose violations are witnessed by finite prefixes of system executions (or traces). For example, a regular expression can be used to encode the pattern of resource acquisition (acq) and release (rel) (rel * ; acq; rel + ) * where a release must follow an acquire, consecutive acquires are disallowed, and extra releases are ignored. As another example, the RTL formula [15] @e 1 + d < @e 2 expresses that event e 2 cannot follow event e 1 within d time units.

div.head: Figure 1. Conceptual Monitoring Architecture
div.p: Conceptually monitoring for such properties involves two activities: generating events and processing events. 1 Figure 1 illustrates these activities for the acquire-release property formulated as a finite state automaton. Statements in tasks that are related to properties being monitored are instrumented, illustrated by dashed boxes, to generate events that reflect the relevant information from the statement, e.g., event acq indicates that a call to acquire was performed. The events are communicated to the monitor which processes each event, e.g., transitioning from the start to the middle state on an acq.

In this paper, we are not concerned with the specific formalism that is used since the notion of predictability of monitoring is orthogonal to formalism. We focus instead on the set of events that may lead directly to a property violation.
Definition 2.1. A Possible Violating Event (PVE) is an event that appears as the last event in some trace that violates a safety property specification.

Under this definition, every state property violation is considered a PVE since failure to satisfy an asserted condition is a violation. For path properties, the situation is more subtle since some events may not be PVEs. For example, in the acquire-release example, acq is a PVE, but rel is not, and in the RTL example, e 2 is a PVE, but e 1 is not. PVEs can be calculated by a simple offline analysis of the property, e.g., for finite state automata symbols that label transitions to a trap state, i.e., a non-accept sink state, are PVEs. We note that accurate runtime monitoring requires that all events, both PVEs and non-PVEs, are processed to drive state transitions; failing to do so may give rise to erroneous reporting of property violations [16].

In predictable runtime monitoring PVEs play a special role. Whenever a PVE occurs a property may have been violated. Ideally, the property monitor would be notified of a PVE's occurrence immediately so that it can determine whether a violation has occurred and, if so, notify the system. PVE notification may be delayed, however, due to, for example, ongoing high-priority system processing. Predictable monitoring requires that this delay is explicitly managed by the run-time system. Definition 2.2. The detection latency (DL) of a property violation is the time between when the violation is manifested in the system and when the monitor detects this violation.

After a violation occurs, the actions needed to mitigate the detected system condition are application-dependent and are not considered in this paper. We note that our definition of violation detection latency does not include the time required for mitigation; we believe that our framework can be extended to account for violation mitigation latency, but we defer that to future work.

For each property a monitor will be defined to process all events that are relevant for the property. When a PVE occurs for a property, it may or may not violate a constraint, so, at least conceptually, the scheduling of monitor processing might vary. If the PVE causes a violation with a detection latency of v time units, then the relative deadline of the monitor for the property is v time units, which includes the time required to process the PVE. For PVE occurrences that do not cause a violation, the monitor job need never be scheduled; the monitor job's deadline could be ∞. Unfortunately, we cannot distinguish these cases statically so we must account for the worst case and enforce v as the monitor deadline for all PVEs.

Non-PVEs must also be processed, as stated previously, but they have no hard deadline. The only deadline requirement for non-PVEs is that that they must be processed before a subsequent PVE can be properly evaluated. Thus, there are a variety of implementation strategies that might be taken in implementing the monitor. It could, for example, process non-PVEs by simply queuing them, effectively deferring their processing until a PVE occurs.

In this paper, we require that the cost of processing a PVE account for the cost of processing any pending non-PVEs; worst-case estimates of the maximum number of non-PVEs between any pair of PVEs in a system may need to be calculated to estimate this cost. Moreover, we assume that the cost of executing any instrumentation added to the system to generate events is accounted for as part of the system execution cost; it is not included in the cost of processing a PVE.

In Section 4.2, we describe asynchronous monitoring techniques wherein separate tasks are used to execute property monitoring. In that case, the PVE processing cost and detection latency for a given property define the timing parameters for the monitor tasks. If a single monitor task is used to check multiple properties with different detection deadlines and costs, then the timing parameters are unclear. There are two ways to resolve this: (1) each task monitors a single property or (2) use fewer tasks than properties where each task conservatively uses the maximum PVE processing cost and the minimum detection latency for its properties as its execution time and deadline. Each approach has its drawbacks. For the first one, the number of monitor tasks may grow to be very large if many properties are monitored and this can negatively impact system performance. For the second one, excessively frequent scheduling may result in poor utilization because of the use of conservative parameters in the schedulability analysis. A compromise can be made between these two schemes. Properties with similar detection deadlines and costs can be clustered into groups and one monitor task used for each such group. Exploration of these implementation strategies is deferred to future work as discussed in Section 7.

Definition 2.3. Given a property p with detection latency l, runtime monitoring is predictable if (a) the monitor can detect all the violations of p in a system within l time units after their occurrence; and (b) the execution of the monitoring job does not affect the original system's schedulability.

div.head: Determining the Monitor Budget
div.p: Under fixed-priority scheduling, a monitor budget is specified by the amount of CPU time, e m , allocated to runtime monitoring during a set period of time, p m . After each p m time units the monitor budget is replenished to a maximum of e m time units. Thus, the term e m defines the execution budget for the monitor, and the term p m defines the replenishment interval for the execution budget. The ratio em pm specifies the share of the CPU allocated to runtime monitoring. In practice, the valuse of e m and p m are usually selected such that em pm ≤ 1. The challenge in determining the monitoring budget, therefore, is more complicated than simply specifying a fraction of the CPU to be allocated to runtime monitoring. An engineer must specify both the execution budget and the replenishment period. Thus, the focus of this section is help determine how to specify these parameters.

The execution budget, e m , is expended processing PVEs. To simplify the presentation in this paper, assume the maximum amount of time to process each PVE, c pve , is the same for all PVEs, and let ρ be the rate at which PVEs will be generated in the system during execution. em pm ≥ ρ•c pve must hold, otherwise the detection latency will be unbounded for a long-running system. To determine the execution budget needed to support runtime monitoring, ρ must be computed.

Unfortunately, there is no universal approach to computing an accurate ρ off-line, as it heavily depends on the program tasks. Moreover, it becomes more complex since the same type of PVEs may be generated by different program tasks. For some applications, there may exist a well-defined interval of p pve time units in which it can be guaranteed that (i) no more than N pve PVEs will be generated and (ii) ρ = N pve /p pve defines a maximum rate at which PVEs will be generated. In this case, the monitor budget should be defined such that Inequality (1) holds.

div.p: In most monitoring schemes, events are generated each time the instrumentation inserted into the code is executed. Consequently, an estimation of N pve can be performed by an off-line analysis of program tasks by considering the monitored properties and the required instrumentation. div.head: Bounding Detection Latency
div.p: Real-time property monitoring requires carefully scheduling the monitor activities to meet two objectives: (1) to satisfy detection latency constraints and (2) to preserve satisfaction of the other timing constraints in the system. In [17], Schroeder divides monitoring approaches into two categories: synchronous monitoring and asynchronous monitoring. In synchronous monitoring, both event generation and processing is embedded in the program tasks. Consequently, event processing is ready to execute immediately after event generation and the challenge, as we discuss below, is not one of achieving detection latency, but one of schedulability in that the detection latency is bounded by the maximum response time of the task being monitoring. In asynchronous monitoring, event generation is also embedded in the program tasks, but event processing is located in separate monitor tasks that are scheduled together with the program tasks.

In the rest of this section, we analysis how different types of monitoring schemes affect the schedulability of the whole system, and present techniques for predicting maximum detection latency (MDL) of PVEs. We focus on monitoring the program tasks, each of which is a periodic task, denoted T i , and executed under fixed-priority scheduling. The task T i has a period p i and execution time e i , which includes the cost of instrumentation. In addition, we assume that the program tasks are sorted by their priorities in decreasing order with the priority of T i greater than that of T i+1 .

div.head: Synchronous Monitoring
div.p: Synchronous monitoring affects the system schedulability in two ways. First, each instrumented task has longer execution time and thus a higher utilization than before it was instrumented. Second, if the embedded event processing code uses some shared resources, resource conflicts may be incurred and thus blocking times are added to the program tasks. If we can estimate the execution time and the blocking time of each instrumented task, then we can use a standard schedulability test on the whole system. If the test indicates that the instrumented tasks are not schedulable, then some measures, e.g. eliminating the monitoring of a property, must be taken to achieve schedulability.
To calculate the MDL of a PVE, we consider two cases: preemptive and non-preemptive event processing.

4.1.1. Preemptive Event Processing. Intuitively, the detection latency of a PVE should be minimal with synchronous monitoring, because the event processing is placed immediately after the PVE in the source code. It turns out, however, that minimal detection latency in synchronous monitoring is only achieved when the event processing the PVE is executed non-preemptively (with the exception of the highest priority task under fixed priority scheduling). If the code is preemptive, then long detection latencies may be incurred.

Consider, for example, task T i that generates PVE pve k at time t k . If another task T j is released just before pve k is processed, the detection of a violation will be delayed by at least e j time units (i.e., the execution time of task T j ). Continuing with this example, in the worst case, every higher priority task could be released and execute (perhaps multiple times, depending on task periods) before the synchronous monitoring code in task T i is able to process pve k .

div.p: 4.1.2. Non-preemptive Event Processing. If the PVE processing is non-preemptive, then it cannot be interrupted by higher-priority tasks during execution, so the detection latency can be minimized to c pve , provided that the code processing this PVE executes immediately and nonpreemptively after the code generating this PVE. This nonpreemptive code introduces, however, "blocking" to higher priority tasks, which must be considered in determining scheduling of the task set. An attractive alternative is to implement asynchronous monitoring, which is discussed in the next section.

div.head: Asynchronous Monitoring
div.p: With asynchronous monitoring, the PVEs are processed by one or more separate monitor tasks. When a PVE occurs, the monitor tasks that process this PVE are released. Since the occurrence of a PVE indicates possible property violations, the monitor task must complete before the detection deadline. If there exist different PVEs with different detection deadlines to be monitored, then multiple monitor tasks may be needed. To simplify the presentation, in this section we assume that all PVEs have the same deadline and detection cost, so only one monitor task is needed.

From the scheduler's point of view, the monitor is simply another task added to the program task set. To achieve predictable monitoring, the monitor task must be scheduled with program tasks appropriately so as to meet two requirements: (1) The whole system is schedulable; (2) The MDL is bounded. To schedule the monitor with the program tasks, the first step is to determine the release pattern of the monitor jobs. a task. Moreover, as was illustrated in Figure 1, the same PVE, e.g., release, may be generated by different tasks.

Figure 3 illustrates three instrumented program tasks, T 1 , T 2 and T 3 generate PVEs that are to be processed by a monitor. A black block in the figure denotes the execution of a task. An upward arrow denotes the release of a task. A downward arrow denotes an occurrence of a PVE and hence the release of a monitor job. The bottom part of the figure shows a fragment of the PVE occurrence pattern (and hence the release pattern of the monitor jobs). As the system is running, this exact pattern is unlikely to reappear. In practice, execution times vary somewhat based on the computation performed, and thus the periods and the execution times in a periodic task model only specify the minimum release times and the maximum execution times of periodic tasks. Release time and execution time jitter will change the actual release pattern of the monitor jobs during execution. The situation is even more complex if the blocking times of the program tasks are taken into consideration. Based on these observations, it is infeasible in practice to model the monitor as a periodic task and specify a minimum release time for it. The aperiodic PVE release pattern brings challenges to predictable monitoring. On the one hand, all PVEs are expected to be processed within their deadlines. On the other hand, the monitor budget allocated to a monitor is limited in most systems. In the following subsection, we discuss a bandwidth-preserving, server-based approach to scheduling monitor tasks with program tasks and show how to compute the PVE MDL with a given monitor budget.

div.head: Bandwidth-preserving Server-based Approach.
div.p: Bandwidth-preserving servers for fixed priority scheduling, such as deferrable servers and sporadic servers, were invented to schedule aperiodic or sporadic tasks [18], [19]. A deferrable server is often characterized by a pair (p m , e m ), where p m is the replenishment period, and e m , the server budget. The ratio U s = em pm is called the server size. Using a server to schedule aperiodic tasks has the advantages that the server budget can be controlled and adjusted by varying aperiodic task response time, while the schedulability of the server and the periodic tasks can be statically analyzed.
Since the monitor task exhibits an aperiodic release pattern, a bandwidth-preserving server can be applied to schedule the monitor to achieve predictable monitoring.

The server budget and period have a direct impact on the schedulability of the whole system, and also determine the capacity of the server to process PVEs. In [18] the authors present two guidelines for designing a deferrable server:

• Assigning the server the highest priority reduces program task response time and increases the chance they will meet their deadlines. • Given a fixed U s , increasing p m reduces the average response time of the aperiodic tasks.

The above two guidelines are applicable while designing a server for predictable monitoring. Assigning the server the highest priority guarantees bounded detection latency, and for some applications it may be helpful to adjust the server period to achieve shorter average detection latency. For predictable monitoring, however, bounding MDL (denoted L M in this section) for a PVE, is a major concern. This leads to additional design criteria for choosing a server period.

• A larger server period tends to negatively impact the schedulability of the whole system, especially for a deferrable server [18]. • A larger server period may be associated with a larger L M , as we shall see in the following discussion.

The tradeoff between schedulability and detection latency is an important design criteria for predictable monitoring and we study some subtleties of this tradeoff in Section 5. In the rest of this section we discuss how to calculate the MDL of PVEs under the following assumptions:

1) The server has the highest priority; 2) All the PVEs have the same detection cost c pve ; 3) They are processed in FIFO order, that is, there is a FIFO event queue holding the PVEs in the system; 4) The server budget e m is a multiple of c pve . 5) The system is schedulable according to the schedulability criteria defined for the bandwidth-preserving server used to implement the monitor.

Given a PVE release pattern and a server, the problem of calculating the MDL of PVEs is in essence to calculate the response time of tasks scheduled by servers. The PVE release pattern assumed in the rest of this paper is that, during any time interval of p pve time units, the maximum number of the PVEs that could occur is no more than N pve . When all the N pve PVEs are released at the same time, the largest MDL is achieved. This is true in that the bandwidthpreserving server's capability to process the PVEs is limited, and by deferring the release of some PVEs to a later time, these PVEs' response times (detection latency) will be reduced. Therefore, to calculate the MDL of the PVEs it suffices to only consider the scenario where all the N pve PVEs of each interval of p pve time units are released at the beginning of this interval.

Again, by the argument in Case 2, we only need to consider the situation where t < LCM (p m , p pve ).

During [0, t), the budget of the server is t pm • e m , and the number of all the released PVEs is t ppve • N pve . The available budget at t is then at most t pm • e m -t ppve • N pve • c pve . On the other hand, the available budget at any time instant during the replenishment period of a deferrable server cannot exceed the length of the interval from this time instant to the beginning of the next replenishment period, i.e. [t, t pm • p m ] for the above scenario where t pm • p m indicates the beginning of the the first replenishment period after t. Therefore the available budget at t is min{ t pm • e m -t ppve • N pve • c pve , t pm • p m -t}. At time t pm • p m , the budget needed to process all the PVEs in the event queue is then equal to
div.formula: l = N pve •c pve -min{ t p m •e m - t p pve •N pve •c pve , t p m •p m -t}(14)
div.p: If l is a multiple of e m , then to process all these PVEs, it will take ( l em -1) complete replenishment periods, plus e m time units. Otherwise, it will take l em complete replenishment periods, plus the time to process the PVEs left after l em replenishment periods, that is, l-l em •e m . Define a function as follows:
div.formula: f (x) = ( x em -1) • p m + e m , x em = x em ; x em • p m + x -x em • e m , otherwise(15)
div.p: The MDL of the PVEs released at t is then
div.formula: mdl(t) = t p m • p m -t + f (l)(16)
div.p: By considering all possible values of t, we can obtain the MDL of all the PVEs:
div.formula: L M = max{mdl(t)|∀t, k ∈ N ∪ {0} : t = k • p pve < LCM (p m , p pve )}(17)

div.head: Trading Latency for Monitoring Budget
div.p: The three cases considered in previous section define how to calculate the MDL of the PVEs when the monitor is scheduled by a bandwidth-preserving server with the highest priority. To achieve predictable monitoring, we need to choose an appropriate server (p m , e m ) such that this server does not affect the schedulability of the program system and the MDL is less than the application-specific detection latency.

In this section, we illustrate tradeoffs that can be made between MDL, the monitoring budget, and the replenishing interval (p m ) via a simulation experiment that uses a deferrable server to schedule the monitor task. The experiment program consists of a deferrable server and ten randomly created target tasks. The priority of the server is higher than those of all the target tasks. During the program execution 180 dummy PVEs with the same detection cost c pve = 1 are generated artificially every 900 time units, that is, N pve = 180, p pve = 900, and all these PVEs are generated with the same release time so as to create the worst-case MDL. Four different server sizes: 0.200, 0.250, 0.333 and 0.500 are studied. For each server size, the value of p m is varied from 120 to 4980 in increments of 60. For each server period, we run the server together with the target task set and then record the MDL of the PVEs. Although we can continue the experiment with more values of p m larger than 5000, it turns out that the changing MDL pattern repeats after 3000, so we only show the results for 120 ≤ p m ≤ 4980. Figure 8 shows the importance of selecting appropriate monitoring budgets and budget replenishment periods for predictable monitoring, and suggests guidelines for designing predictable monitors.

As expected and shown in Figure 8, for each given p m , the MDL of a larger server size is always no greater than that of a smaller server size. In some cases, however, a larger server size yields the same MDL as that achievable with a smaller server size. So, for these cases, increasing the server size does not help in reducing the MDL. Nonetheless, larger server sizes do result in more replenishment intervals that minimize the MDL of the PVEs.

Unfortunately, the share of the CPU that can be allocated to runtime monitoring is often limited in practice. Under this situation, selecting the replenishment period becomes a critical step in designing predictable monitors. Generally speaking, the replenishment period impacts predictable monitoring in several aspects, e.g., the schedulability of the whole system, the average detection latency and the MDL of the PVEs. For instance, with a fixed size deferrable server a longer server period generally leads to shorter average detection latency, but it also is more likely to affect the schedulability of the whole system [18].

An interesting finding from this study is that a shorter average detection latency does not necessarily lead to a lower MDL. Consider the case when the sever size is 0.200 in Figure 8. The lowest MDL is achieved when p m is a multiple of p pve , and even if p m increases by a small value, the MDL will go up drastically. As p m continues to increase, the MDL fluctuates. For example, when p m = 900, the MDL is less then 200; but when p m = 960, the MDL increases to a value over 800. As p m increases, the MDL may fluctuate. The trend in the simulation suggests that if a bandwidthpreserving server is used to schedule the monitor, then it is desirable to let p m be a multiple of p pve .

Figure 8 also shows that, when the server size is fixed, a small p m should be avoided in most cases. When the server size is 0.250, 0.333 or 0.500, the MDL is near its maximum if p m has a small value, e.g. 120. This is because a small replenishment period creates significant dispersal of the monitor budget.

It is necessary to emphasize that the MDL is influenced by multiple factors, such as the PVE release pattern, the monitoring budget, the replenishment period, and the monitoring schemes (e.g., the monitor priority, the consumption and the replenishment policy). Further study is needed to fully characterize those influences, but this preliminary study suggests that the subtle interactions between choices of these parameters must be considered when configuring predictable monitoring schemes.

Finally, for the case where the server size is 0.200, we compare the MDLs measured in the experiment and the one calculated by our analysis and by Equation (7). We compared all the values of p m used in our experiment, but due to space restrictions, only a subset of them is listed in Table 1. In Table 1, M DL 1 , M DL 2 and M DL 3 are the MDLs obtained by the simulation, by our analysis, and by Equation ( 7) respectively. As can be seen from this table, while Equation ( 7) produces pessimistic results, the MDLs calculated by our analysis match the experimental results tightly.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Significant research has been conducted on developing software-based dynamic monitoring techniques and reducing their overhead on the monitored systems. Chodrow et al. implemented a run-time environment based on Real-Time Logic (RTL) [15] for specifying and monitoring real-time system [22]. Mok and Liu extended Chodrow et al.'s work by giving an algorithm for violation detection and developing a Java run-time timing constraint monitor (JRTM) [23], [24]. In [25], Kim et al. describe Java-MaC, a runtime verification system for Java programs based on the Monitoring and Checking (MaC) architecture [26]. In [27] the authors present an automata-based approach for run-time program checking against Linear Temporal Logic specifications. Their algorithm is implemented using an observer generator tool which has been integrated into Java PathExplorer, a generic run-time verification framework [28].

In all these software-based monitoring approaches, a monitor is another task in the system which contends for the processor and shares resources with the program tasks. The monitor also needs to be scheduled with the program tasks so as to respect their deadlines in a real-time system. All the above work focuses on either the formal methods for dynamic monitoring or reducing the monitoring overhead, but none of them have taken into consideration the monitor's deadlines and the schedulability of the whole system.

On the other hand, in real-time scheduling theory literature, Liu and Layland's work [29] laid solid foundation for scheduling periodic tasks in hard real-time environments. To schedule aperiodic or sporadic tasks, server algorithms have been proposed [18], [19], [30].

There are significant and growing research bodies on both dynamic monitoring and real-time scheduling. However, little attention has been paid on the marriage between these two fields for predictable monitoring. To the best of our knowledge, our's is the first work on this subject.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper, we introduced the concept of predictable monitoring. We defined two conditions, temporal noninterference and bounded detection latency, that should govern how runtime monitoring is integrated into a realtime system. To realize predictable monitoring schemes we present the concepts of monitoring budgets and violation detection latency specifications. With these quantities we explored both synchronous and asynchronous strategies for performing runtime monitoring under fixed-priority scheduling and we studied the conditions under which that monitoring is predictable. Using simulation, we explored the tradeoff between the period of a bandwidth-preserving server and detection latency and observe that there are some subtleties in the wise selection of parameters for predictable monitoring schemes.

In future work, we plan to extend our approach to make it more general, by clustering properties with similar scheduling parameters into monitor tasks, and to integrate recently developed techniques that dynamically enable and disable event generation to minimize monitoring overhead, e.g., [31]. These techniques make it possible that a location in a program task may or may not generate a PVE when executed, depending on the state of the property monitor. This will require a novel approach accounting for PVEs in order to avoid overly pessimistic scheduling parameters.
